facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: This group of sanctuaries, founded by the Pallava kings, was carved out of rock along the Coromandel coast in the 7th and 8th centuries.
facts.text: UNESCO inscribed the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram on the World Heritage List in 1984, recognizing the Pallava dynasty rock-cut sanctuaries and structural temples along the Coromandel coast.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: About three of the clock the next morning we came to a place, which is called the Seven Pagodas, upon which are eight pleasant hillocks...
facts.source_name: Seven Pagodas of Mahabalipuram (Wikipedia citing Balbi, 1590)
facts.text: Venetian merchant Gasparo Balbi recorded the earliest known European reference naming the coastal site Seven Pagodas in 1590.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The myths tell of six temples submerged beneath the waves with the seventh temple – the Mahabalipuram temple – still standing on the seashore.
facts.source_name: Seven Pagodas of Mahabalipuram (Wikipedia citing Goldingham, 1798)
facts.text: British surveyor John Goldingham documented a popular local account in 1798 alleging that six grand temples were submerged by an ocean deluge, leaving only one standing on the shore.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: the more aged people among them, remembered to have seen the tops of several Pagodas far out in the sea, which being covered with copper (probably gilt) were particularly brilliant
facts.source_name: Seven Pagodas of Mahabalipuram (Wikipedia citing Chambers, 1788)
facts.text: Eighteenth-century colonial accounts documented local assertions that the glittering copper pinnacles of sunken temples were formerly visible offshore to mariners.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Just before the tsunami waves struck on December 26, 2004, the sea withdrew about 500 metres, baring its bed on which lay a temple structure and several rock sculptures.
facts.text: During the Indian Ocean tsunami on December 26, 2004, the sea temporarily withdrew approximately 500 metres offshore at Mahabalipuram, briefly exposing submerged granite masonry to onlookers.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Among the tsunami 'gifts' found in Mahabalipuram... are the remnants of a stone house and a half-completed rock elephant... There are also two giant granite lions.
facts.text: Post-tsunami sand scouring on the Mahabalipuram beachfront in 2005 exposed buried seventh-century Pallava granite sculptures, including a monolithic lion, an elephant, and a stallion.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: After the recession of the coastline following the tsunami, archaeologists identified several stone structures buried in the sand close to the Mahabalipuram temple.
facts.text: Archaeological Survey of India excavations immediately south of the Shore Temple revealed the basement of an ancient structural shrine and dressed stone alignments that had been buried in sand.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: It is a structural temple, built with blocks of granite, dating from the 8th century AD. At the time of its creation, the site was a busy port during the reign of Narasimhavarman II of the Indian Pallava dynasty.
facts.text: Architectural and epigraphical records date the construction of the standing structural Shore Temple to the reign of Pallava king Narasimhavarman II between 700 and 728 CE.
